name: Pendulum Squat
tierNote: Safety tier B (content.md 5.1: machine-guided spinal load, hack and pendulum); census.json difficulty tier 1.

claims.text: Set the machine so the shoulders sit under the pads and the feet are on the platform.

quotes.text: Adjust the machine so you can position your shoulders under the pads and feet on the platform.

claims.text: Feet about hip-width apart on the platform (StrengthLog); a gym's trainers use about shoulder-width with the toes turned out slightly.

quotes.text: Place your feet slightly about hip-width apart on the platform.
Feet are positioned roughly shoulder-width apart, toes angled out slightly to match individual hip anatomy.

claims.text: Brace (engage) the core and keep the back pressed against the backrest the whole time.

quotes.text: Engage your core and keep your back pressed against the backrest throughout the movement.
Before you move, lightly brace your core.

claims.text: Release the safety latch and lower slowly by bending the knees until the thighs are parallel to the floor or a little lower.

quotes.text: Release the safety latch and lower yourself slowly by bending your knees until your thighs are parallel to the floor or slightly lower.

claims.text: Push back up through the heels, straightening the knees, torso upright throughout.

quotes.text: Push back to the starting position by pushing through your heels and extend your knees. Remember to keep your torso upright during the entire movement.

claims.text: On the way down the knees bend, the hips sink, the torso stays upright and the knees track over the toes; go as deep as the machine and your mobility allow, thighs at or below parallel.

quotes.text: The knees bend and the hips sink into the deep squat position. The torso remains upright the arc of the machine naturally maintains this position. The knees track over the toes throughout.
Descend as deeply as the machine allows and mobility permits the goal is to reach a position where the thighs are at or below parallel to the floor.

claims.text: Drive up through the whole foot, heel and ball.

quotes.text: Push through the full foot heel and ball driving back up through the pendulum arc to the starting position.

claims.text: Knees caving inward: drive them out in line with the toes, and reduce the load if it keeps happening.

quotes.text: Knees caving inward: Valgus collapse at the knee during the descent or ascent. Fix: actively drive the knees outward in line with the toes throughout. Reduce load if the collapse persists.

claims.text: Heels rising, from limited ankle mobility: raise the heels slightly on a plate or wedge while the ankles improve.

quotes.text: Heels rising: Insufficient ankle mobility prevents the heels staying flat through the full depth. Fix: elevate the heels slightly on a plate or wedge while ankle mobility is developed.

claims.text: Dropping into the bottom instead of controlling the descent: lower over two to three seconds every rep.

quotes.text: Rushing the descent: Dropping into the bottom rather than controlling the lowering phase. Fix: a controlled two to three second descent on every rep.

claims.text: Stopping short of parallel misses the hardest part; reduce the load and go to full depth.

quotes.text: Not reaching full depth: Stopping the descent before parallel, missing the most demanding portion of the movement. Fix: reduce load and descend to full depth.

claims.text: The quads work most (the primary driver); the glutes, adductors and hamstrings help.

quotes.text: Primary muscles worked: Quads Glutes Adductors
Primary: Quadriceps all four heads, with particularly significant emphasis on the rectus femoris and vastus lateralis due to the upright torso and deep range of motion.
Secondary: Gluteus maximus, hamstrings, adductors, gastrocnemius (knee stability).
The quads are the primary driver.

claims.text: It isolates the quads with little pressure on the back, in a guided path.

quotes.text: The pendulum squat is an effective exercise for isolating the quadriceps with minimal pressure on the back. The stabilized movement path of the machine allows for full control throughout, making it a safe and joint-friendly option.

claims.text: Typical sets: 8 to 12 reps at a challenging load through full range; a deeper squat at the same load counts as progress.

quotes.text: Sets of 8 to 12 repetitions at a challenging load, through full range, are the standard approach for strength and hypertrophy.
Depth consistency is tracked alongside load a deeper squat at the same load is meaningful progress, not just load increase.

claims.text: Lifting the heels shifts the weight forward and strains the knees; bouncing at the bottom risks injury; knees caving on the way up stress the knee joints.

quotes.text: Lifting heels off the platform during the descent. This shifts weight forward and strains your knees. Keep your whole foot planted.
Bouncing at the bottom of the movement. This uses momentum instead of muscle and risks injury. Control the transition smoothly.
Letting knees cave inward during the ascent. This stresses your knee joints and limits glute activation. Push knees out actively.

claims.text: Grip the handles firmly.

quotes.text: Grip handles firmly.

claims.text: After the last rep, return to the top, lock the safety, check that it holds the weight, then step out; learn how the safety works before you start.

quotes.text: Once you’ve hit your rep count, re-engage the safety and make sure it’s on before attempting to get off the machine.
It’s a good idea to check before you get on the machine how the stopper/safety works, so you can do it easily when you reach this point.
After your final rep, return to the top and make sure you are stable.
Before stepping out, check that the weight is fully supported.
Stand tall → engage the safety → confirm it is locked → step out.

claims.text: Tempo: FORM's trainers ask for a controlled two to three second descent and XcelerateGyms (a gym blog) counts three seconds down; no pendulum source gives seconds for the lifting phase, so the plate's 1 s up is a drawing convention.

quotes.text: Rushing the descent: Dropping into the bottom rather than controlling the lowering phase. Fix: a controlled two to three second descent on every rep.
Lower slowly by bending your knees, counting three seconds down.
quotes.where: Step 3: How to Lower Safely (Controlled Eccentric)

claims.text: At the bottom, pause for a second, then drive the feet into the foot plate to stand; keep the movement controlled, not explosive.

quotes.text: Once you’re at the bottom of your squat, pause for a second, and then drive your feet into the foot plate to push yourself up again.
Aim for a controlled movement—there’s no need to be explosive.

claims.text: A machine maker's guide says not to drop quickly to the bottom but to lower under control, and that it often sees people add too much weight and then lose control on the way down.

quotes.text: Do not drop quickly to the bottom. Lower yourself under control.
In my decades of design experience, I often see people add too much weight and then lose control on the way down.

claims.text: At the top, don't snap the knees straight aggressively: extend fully without locking out hard (the second line is from a gym blog, WEAK).

quotes.text: Do not aggressively snap your knees straight at the top.
Extend fully at the top without locking out hard.
quotes.where: Step 5: Driving Up with Correct Form

claims.text: A way out: know how the safety catch works so you can engage it mid-movement; it gives you a way out if you fail a rep.

quotes.text: Make sure you’re very familiar with how the safety catch works in case you need to engage it mid-movement.
quotes.where: Common Mistakes: Not Knowing How the Safety Lever Works

quotes.text: Plus, it features a safety catch that gives you an “out” if you fail a rep, unlike traditional squats.

plate.viewWhy: Depth (thighs to parallel, c4, c6), the back on the pad (c3), the upright torso (c5) and the heels lifting (c9) are sagittal.
plate.equipment: Pendulum squat machine (census need pendulum, missing): swinging arm on a pivot with shoulder pads and a back pad, a fixed foot platform, handles and a safety latch (c1, c4). Floor line.
plate.frames: Rep convention: start standing at the top of the arc, end at the bottom (thighs parallel or lower); Trace follows the knee.
plate.start: Standing on the platform, shoulders under the pads, back against the back pad (c1, c3); feet about hip- to shoulder-width (c2); latch released (c4).
plate.end: Knees bent, thighs parallel to the floor or a little lower (c4, c6); knees over the toes (c6); torso upright and back on the pad (c3, c5); heels flat (c9).

checkpoints.label: Back on pad
checkpoints.what: Core braced, back pressed against the backrest.

checkpoints.label: Thighs to parallel
checkpoints.what: Lower until your thighs are parallel or a little lower.

checkpoints.label: Knees over toes
checkpoints.what: Knees track over the toes, never caving in.

mistake.what: Heels lift off the platform at the bottom.
mistake.why: The top fault, losing control and dropping into the bottom (c20, c10), is seen only as speed, so the plate draws the next fault by the same steps: heels lifting. FORM's trainers list it, from limited ankle mobility (c9); XcelerateGyms says it shifts the weight forward and strains the knees (c15).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 1: losing control and dropping into the bottom (c20, c10). Step 1 hit: YR Fitness's "In my decades of design experience, I often see people add too much weight and then lose control on the way down." (c20). 'often see people' is a frequency word for a fault of this exercise; the load half is a load choice and is set aside, as R-LB6-5 read 'most people ... put more weight on the machine than they can handle and rush through the movement'. It is the only step-1 hit, so it is the top fault (FORM's 'Rushing the descent: Dropping into the bottom', c10). Set aside at step 1: YR's "rushing the descent often makes the rep harder to control" (what rushing does, not how often it happens; the same fault), "For many people, lowering until the thighs reach or pass roughly parallel can feel natural." (depth comfort, not a fault) and "I usually recommend one light practice set before moving to your normal working weight." (setup); FORM's "Clients who struggle to feel their quads during compound lower body work often find the pendulum squat provides immediate and clear quad stimulus" and "A common challenge for clients earlier in their training is failing to feel the target muscles during compound exercises" (muscle feel) and "one of the least common" (the machine); BoxLife's "its biggest disadvantage is that it’s not common" (the machine), "In many cases, it’s due to either hip immobility or ankle inflexibility" (the barbell squat), "what you usually squat" (the load) and "The leg press machine is a much more common squat variation than the pendulum" (another exercise). StrengthLog and XcelerateGyms have no frequency word for a fault; 'Common Faults', 'Common Mistakes to Avoid' and 'the most common questions' are headings or list sentences. drawable false: losing control on the way down is seen only as speed (LR-31). The plate draws the next fault by the same steps, heels lifting (c9, c15). Step 2 among the rest: three named faults are tied to harm, each by XcelerateGyms only (WEAK) and each on its common-mistakes list: heels lifting ("This shifts weight forward and strains your knees.", c15), knees caving ("This stresses your knee joints and limits glute activation.", c15) and bouncing at the bottom ("This uses momentum instead of muscle and risks injury.", c15). The two lists that name heels and knees give opposite orders (FORM: knees first; XcelerateGyms: heels first), so step 3's count decides (D-SUP-LB6-CCP), the read sources that tell the lifter to avoid each: heels lifting 4 (FORM c9; XcelerateGyms c15; BoxLife's "It’s important that you find the right platform angle for you, because you don’t want your heels to lift off the platform as you squat." and "You should be squatting as low as you can go without your heels lifting off the platform.", one source; YR's "Stop going deeper if: Your heels start lifting."); knees caving 3 (FORM, XcelerateGyms, YR's "Avoid letting your knees collapse inward."); bouncing 2 (XcelerateGyms, YR's "Avoid bouncing out of the bottom."). Lines that only give the right position are not counted ("Keep your feet flat.", "Keep heels down at the bottom.", "Full foot contact on the platform"). Heels lifting is the next fault, and the side view shows it, so plate.mistake is heels lifting (R-LB8-6). handlingMistakes after the top fault: heels lifting, then knees caving; "Stopping above parallel" (c11) leaves the list, as no source ties it to harm, and the "Thighs to parallel" checkpoint keeps the depth. Set aside at step 2: XcelerateGyms' "Speed reduces time under tension and increases injury risk." (rushing, the top fault itself) and its list sentence "Watch out for these five form errors that limit your results and increase injury risk."; BoxLife's list sentence "But if you do it wrong, you could be missing out on the benefits and increasing your chance of injury.", its 'Forgetting to Adjust It' ("can be both ineffective and dangerous"; a setup choice), 'Lifting Too Heavy' (the load) and 'Not Knowing How the Safety Lever Works' ("without hurting yourself"; not a position during the set), and its "Control the descent and you’ll be able to do the movement more safely" ('safely' is not a harm word); XcelerateGyms' "Stop if you feel pain or pinching." and YR's "What if you feel pain? Stop the exercise rather than trying to push through it." name no fault. Pick changed from the head (written before LR-31): handlingMistakes[0] was knees caving and drawable was true; now the top fault is dropping into the bottom, drawable false, and the plate still draws heels lifting. Scan completion (fetcher scan, 2026-10-22), also set aside: YR's "A lighter, smoother rep is usually a better place to start." (the load); XcelerateGyms' "I’ll break down each step so you can avoid the mistakes I made early on." (no frequency word), "Safer for beginners learning squat mechanics." and "Yes, beginners can safely use this machine." (the exercise) and "The upright torso position puts all stress directly on your legs." (the machine); BoxLife's "there’s also more room for error here as you have no back support" (the Smith machine squat, another exercise), "it could save you pain and improve your range of motion" (setting the machine, a setup choice), and its back-support and joint lines ("there’s little chance of hurting it with poor form", "You may even be able to reduce joint pain this way.") are about the machine, not a fault; YR's "Mayo Clinic advises stopping a strength exercise if it causes pain and considering a lower weight or another attempt after recovery." and XcelerateGyms' "Stop if you feel pain or pinching." name no fault (no shown line uses them). FORM's 'clients ... typically standing on the foot platform' is setup.

tells.text: Back stays pressed to the pad
Whole foot stays on the platform

tempo.text: Down 3: FORM's trainers ask for a controlled two to three second descent on every rep (c10, copied in c18) and XcelerateGyms counts three seconds down (c18); 3 is inside FORM's range and matches the count, each from a source that fixes the lowering phase (R-LB2-1). Up 1 is a drawing convention: no pendulum source fixes the seconds of the lifting phase (c18, WEAK). XcelerateGyms' '3-1-2-0 tempo' has no order key on its page, so it is not read. Pause 0: no quote asks for a pause right after the push up (LR-33); YR's 'Return to the starting position under control, then begin your next rep.' asks none. BoxLife's 'pause for a second' sits at the bottom (c19), so it is named here and not written in pause; XcelerateGyms' 'Hold breath briefly at the bottom' is a breath hold at the bottom.

grip.type: Hands on the machine's handles, gripped firmly (c16).
grip.note: Hand archetype balance. Only a weak blog line supports the grip; no source on hand position.

setup.step: Set the machine so your shoulders sit under the pads and your feet are on the platform.
Feet hip- to shoulder-width. Brace and press your back into the pad.
Release the safety latch and lower slowly until your thighs are at least parallel.
Push up through your whole foot. After the last rep, lock the safety and check it holds before you step out.
If you fail a rep, the safety catch gives you an out.

posture.point: Extend fully at the top, without locking out hard.

handlingMistakes.fix: Lower over two to three seconds.
Drive them out over your toes; go lighter if it keeps happening.

rows.means: Your quads are the primary driver.
Knees caving in or heels lifting puts strain on the knees.
rows.fix: Knees over your toes, whole foot down. Reduce load if the collapse persists.

risks.risk: Knees caving in on the way up stresses the knee joints.
Heels lifting shifts your weight forward and strains your knees.
Bouncing out of the bottom can cause injury.

zooms.right: Knees in line with the toes.

libraryDiff.why: Library: quads primary; glutes and hamstrings secondary. StrengthLog lists quads, glutes and adductors; FORM's trainers put the quads first and list glutes, hamstrings, adductors and calves as secondary (c12). Adductors are proposed as a secondary. A proposal for the LIB data card.

anchorNote: StrengthLog's pendulum squat page (short) and FORM gym's trainer page read in full; the XcelerateGyms blog was read in full and is used only for risk consequences and the grip line (WEAK). No ACE or NASM page exists (NASM URL 404, 2026-10-02); PubMed has no pendulum-squat paper (9 hits, none on the machine). T Nation and MuscleWiki returned 403.

loadProgression.text: Sets of 8 to 12 at a challenging load through full range; a deeper squat at the same load is progress too.

unsourced: Breathing: only XcelerateGyms (a gym blog) gives one (breathe in on the way down, hold briefly at the bottom, out on the way up); no claim was added in the LB8 pass.
Foot height on the platform for quad vs glute emphasis (search snippets only).
